The ninth-century Persian geographer Ibn Khordadbeh records it as a typical instrument of Byzantium; the oldest image is on an ivory box of about 900 to 1100. It spread along Byzantine trade routes, and European writers of the eleventh and twelfth centuries used the words fiddle and lyre for each other. The instrument is regarded as one of the ancestors of European bowed instruments and influenced the medieval rebec and the Italian lira da braccio; modern variants are still found in the Balkans and around the Black Sea.

The Byzantine lyra is a bowed instrument of the medieval Byzantine Empire, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-71. Its common form has a pear-shaped body and three to five strings, and it is held upright and played by touching the strings from the side with the fingertips and nails. In organology it belongs to the family of bowed lutes. Modern variants are still used in the Balkans and around the Black Sea, including in Greece, Crete, Karpathos, Albania, Montenegro, Serbia, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Croatia, Italy, Turkey and Armenia.
拜占庭里拉琴音色溫潤而富有穿透力，具有獨特的中世紀弦樂特徵。其音質介於明亮與暗沉: The Byzantine lyra has a warm, carrying timbre with the particular character of medieval strings. Its quality lies between bright and dark, with a warm sheen of overtones. Because the number of strings is limited its range is fairly narrow, mostly in the middle register, where it can set out a clear melodic line. The small vibration of the bow sets the air in the resonator going naturally, which gives the tone a soft, nasal quality. Beside the modern violin the lyra is plainer and more inward, with a touch of age and bleakness; beside the bright tinkle of a harp it has more depth and more song. Its sound reflects the aesthetic character of medieval Byzantine instruments.
